finding.claim: POST /profile/avatar fetches an attacker-supplied URL. The only check is that the value is a string starting with 'https://'. The host, resolved IP, and redirect targets are not validated, so the server can be made to request internal HTTPS hosts and, via axios's default redirect-following, internal HTTP targets such as 169.254.169.254.

trace.note: app.post('/profile/avatar') registered with no auth middleware
url = req.body.avatarUrl taken directly from the request body
only typeof === 'string' and startsWith('https://') checked; no host, IP, port, or redirect validation
axios.get issued with default redirect following; no maxRedirects:0, no timeout, no maxContentLength
response returned only as img.data.length, which leaks response size

finding.guards_checked: Scheme check at server.js:11 (bypassable via redirect and does not constrain host). No IP/host allowlist, no DNS resolution check, no post-redirect re-validation, no auth check on the route. Redirect default is from axios's documented config; the repo has no package.json or lockfile to pin the version.

verdict.guard_found: Only the scheme check at server.js:11 (typeof string and startsWith('https://')). It does not constrain host, IP, or redirects. No auth middleware on the route (server.js:9), and no maxRedirects:0, timeout, or maxContentLength on the axios call at server.js:14. No other validation exists in server.js, and it is the only file in the directory.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: server.js:9 has no auth, server.js:10 reads req.body.avatarUrl, server.js:11 is a scheme-only check, and server.js:14 calls axios.get(url) with default redirect following, so an attacker-supplied https URL can reach internal hosts or redirect to internal HTTP targets, with the response size returned at server.js:15. The only uncertainty is the axios version, since no package.json or lockfile is present, but the default redirect-following behavior is long-standing.
